turn_text: Well, and as you were saying, in this situation, timing is crucial here. And so I'm wondering, what are some of the sticking points you expect between the House and Senate as they work to sort of come to an agreement on this legislation?

The House and Senate actually have similar structures in a number of ways in their bills. And as I often say, they're singing off the same song sheet, but they have different lyrics. And one of the areas where they're quite a bit different is in the passenger space. Those small businesses and some of the pastors are large that report their income on an individual basis. And the Senator Hatch just released some changes last night, rather late, where he's actually making it easier for people who are in pass through businesses to take advantage of the lower pass, special pass through rate that they have in the Senate bill. I think that area is a challenge for both the House and Senator reconcile the approaches they have there. The other area that I think there's a pretty significant difference is, well, the structure of the international reform is the same. It both have very different approaches to what we call base erosion, which is If we move to this modernized international tax system, how do we protect from companies shifting profits overseas? And that, I think, is a very complex area of tax law, and they have different approaches, and they're going to have to resolve those at the end of the day. The other issue that is more significant in the Senate and the House is obviously having legislation that meets this requirement for reconciliation. As we know, because they're using a tool that's typically used for budget processes, this legislation cannot legislate. It has to have a budget impact for whichever provision you have and cannot increase the deficit outside the tenure window. I know that the new mark that Senator Hatch introduced last night is an attempt to address that. That's why they're looking at the individual mandate. And in the Senate, they're not looking at repealing the individual mandate, and it's actually making certain that there is no tax for failing to sign up for health insurance. That raises well over $300 billion in revenue, and so I think that's very appealing to the Senate. And then lastly, I would say the issue that's gotten the most attention, but I think can be resolved is what to do on the state and local tax deduction. That's one of the issues a lot of members are concerned about on a regional basis for both parties. And the Senate completely repeals the ability to deduct state and local taxes. The House has a provision that allows the deduction of property taxes up to $10,000. So they're going to have to figure out a way to resolve it. And I think a total repeal would have difficulty passing the House at this point. So that's one of the more visible areas that has gained a lot of press attention that they're going to have to resolve.
